lines: In a robot cell or a CNC machine, the application that commands a motor can crash.
When it does, the motor must not keep acting on its last command, and the rest of the machine must keep running.
EtherQ is an open-source EtherCAT master for QNX 8.0.
It ports the SOEM master to QNX, runs it in an independent daemon, and exposes the bus as a QNX resource manager under slash dev slash ecat.
Here it runs on real QNX 8.0 in QEMU, against three simulated EtherCAT devices.
Upstream SOEM, compiled for QNX, finds all three slaves through the io-sock packet filter.
The EtherQ daemon brings the bus to operational. Its cycle is driven by a QNX timer pulse, at a fixed real-time priority.
Now a separate process, axisdemo, enables the servo through the CiA 402 sequence, and drives it along a smooth profile.
Watch what happens when we kill it with SIGKILL.
No cleanup code runs in the client. But QNX closes its connection to the resource manager, and EtherQ zeroes the six output bytes it owned, and releases them.
The servo drops to switch on disabled, while the bus stays operational.
Every output byte has exactly one owner. A second writer gets: resource busy.
If the master itself stops for one second, the devices' watchdogs drop them to safe operational, and the supervisor recovers the bus as soon as it resumes.
The daemon can also drop root after start-up, and keep running as an ordinary user, with locked QNX abilities.
This is a real QNX 8.0 build, with the QNX compiler, and zero warnings.
The safe stop is a few lines in the close handler.
And an automated end-to-end test on the QNX target passes every check.
EtherQ brings open-source EtherCAT to QNX, with crash-safe outputs by design.
Next step: validation on physical EtherCAT hardware.
